title: The evidence museum
subtitle: Review • Fossils, soils and light
objective: Use evidence to correct museum labels about fossils, soils and light.

sow.exactOutcome: Review and evidence learning on fossils, soils & light (Entry Level Science / UAS).
sow.alignment: Chronological continuation of the supplied SOW. This lesson develops or reviews the named outcome; it does not claim an accreditation award.

priorLearning: Fossils can preserve evidence of past living things.
Light must reach an eye for sight.
success: Use a clue from each science strand.
State one thing the evidence cannot tell us.

vocabulary.meaning: Preserved remains or traces of ancient life.
A mixture that includes mineral and organic material.
Send arriving light back from a surface.
Information that supports or challenges an idea.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one chosen pupil route; pencil; optional ruler; projector or offline HTML.
preparation: Print the shared evidence, one response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the worked answers. Prepare an oral, pointing or adult-scribed route where useful.
Use this as an honest synthesis and evidence review, not a claim that these topics are all new. Optional clean sealed samples may support observation.
safety: No digging, tasting, crumbling fossils or handling unknown soil is required. Use printed evidence or clean sealed samples.
If using a lamp, use a cool low-power LED and keep it away from eyes. Never view the Sun.
practicalAlternative: All core reasoning uses the supplied evidence and can be completed in 40 minutes without a live practical.

misconceptions.correction: A fossil is preserved evidence of past life; a stone alone need not contain this evidence.
misconceptions.check: Ask what evidence of life is present.

misconceptions.correction: Soil also contains organic matter and spaces with air or water.
misconceptions.check: Ask which card shows a non-mineral component.

misconceptions.claim: An eye lights up an exhibit.
misconceptions.correction: Light enters the eye from the lit exhibit.
misconceptions.check: Trace the arrow at the eye.

access.supported: Short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed reasons; same core scientific goal.
access.standard: Make a short evidence-based explanation or record using the supplied information.
access.stretch: Apply the core idea to a changed case, evaluate evidence or identify a limit.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer seated observation, quiet paired rehearsal, private feedback and a pass from public sharing. Routes respond to current access needs, not a diagnosis.

slides.title: The museum has three doubtful labels
body: Keep a claim only if the clues support it.
slides.notes: Read the objective. Pupils may edit by choosing, pointing or writing; each route uses all three strands.

slides.title: Retrieve one idea from each strand
body: 1. What can a fossil be evidence of?
3. Do eyes receive or make viewing light?
slides.notes: Accept ancient life; mineral grains, organic matter, air, water or organisms; eyes receive light. Record uncertainty for review.

slides.title: I separate a fossil from a model
body: Today’s imprint can model a shape.
The model does not become ancient.
slides.notes: Think aloud: “A has a geological history. B was made today. Similar shape does not mean the same origin.” A fossil need not preserve every feature of an organism.

visual.title: From living thing to preserved evidence
visual.description: A simplified three-stage sequence: shell-bearing animal dies, sediment buries its shell, and much later a shell fossil is preserved in rock. This is one possible route, not every fossil.

elements.text: Much time passes. Most remains do not become fossils.

slides.title: I repair the soil label
body: Spaces can contain air or water.
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “Card C lists decayed leaf fragments. That single clue defeats the word only in ‘soil is only rock’.” The diagram is not a measured recipe.

visual.title: Soil is a mixture
visual.description: Enlarged schematic components of soil: mineral particles, organic matter and pore spaces containing air or water. Positions and sizes are illustrative, not measured proportions.

elements.text:
Organic matter:
remains of living things

Spaces can hold
air and water.
Not to scale. Living organisms can also occur in soil.

slides.title: I follow the museum light
body: Follow reflected light into the eye.
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “The fossil is not making light. I trace both arrows to the same lit surface.” An ordinary object can be visible with reflected light.

visual.title: The exhibit needs a light path
visual.description: The lamp emits light onto the top surface of an opaque fossil exhibit; reflected light leaves that same lit surface and enters the eye. The eye is above the object surface.

elements.text:
Some reflected light
enters the eye.
A plain fossil is a reflector, not a light source.

slides.title: Curators compare A and B
slides.notes: Prediction partners choose first, then read the card evidence. W1: A fossil; B model. Neither card reveals the ancient shell’s exact original colour.

slides.title: Repair the two-word traps
slides.notes: W2: Soil is a mixture including mineral and organic material. Eyes receive light; the lamp is the source. Use cards C–E and diagrams. Reveal after a pupil commits to a correction.
slides.reveal: Use the given components and the lamp → exhibit → eye path.

slides.title: Which label can stay?
slides.notes: Correct second option. Re-teach evidence versus appearance if the fossil/model distinction is insecure.

options.text: Today’s clay imprint is an ancient fossil.
options.feedback: Its known history is a model made today.

options.text: The fossil can be seen when reflected light reaches the eye.
options.feedback: This matches the light path in D.
Card C records decayed leaf fragments.

slides.title: Choose your science route
slides.notes: Set ONE route. Use one route with the shared records. Credit a accurate spoken museum label equally to a written label. Check that each claim has a specific clue.

slides.title: Make your own evidence record
slides.notes: Use one route with the shared records. Credit a accurate spoken museum label equally to a written label. Check that each claim has a specific clue.

slides.title: Check what the evidence can show
body: Point to the clue you used.
slides.notes: Shares independent time. Ask for a reason, not just a correct word. Use one route with the shared records. Credit a accurate spoken museum label equally to a written label. Check that each claim has a specific clue.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve the shared account
slides.notes: Listen to a selected pupil revision and visibly adopt a scientifically accurate contribution. Offer private, written or partner feedback.
slides.prompt: Which word did our evidence make us change?
slides.reveal: Words such as only, every or disappeared can go beyond the evidence.

slides.title: Keep the useful change
slides.notes: Shares review time. Name how a pupil contribution changed a label, method or conclusion. Do not rank pupils.
slides.reveal: Words such as only, every or disappeared can go beyond the evidence.

slides.title: Three final checks
body: E1. What does a fossil preserve?
E2. Name one non-mineral part of soil.
E3. What must enter the eye to see the exhibit?
slides.notes: Collect brief individual evidence. Use the answer key and re-teach the specified misconception if needed.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence • Museum records
pupilPages.intro: Fictional records for review. Use the history and observations, not just an object’s name.

cards.title: A • Ancient shell
cards.text: A geologist identifies a preserved shell in old sedimentary rock. Its original colour is unknown.

cards.title: B • Model imprint
cards.text: A pupil pressed a modern shell into clay today. It models an imprint; it is not an ancient fossil.

cards.title: C • Soil sample
cards.text: Observed: mineral grains, dark decayed leaf fragments and spaces. Some spaces contain water or air.

cards.title: D • Lit display
cards.text: A lamp lights the fossil. Some reflected light enters a visitor’s eye.

cards.title: E • Complete darkness
cards.text: Same fossil, but all light is excluded. The eye receives no light from it.

blocks.prompt: W1. Which record is an ancient fossil, and which is a model? Why?
W2. Repair “soil is only rock” or “eyes make viewing light”.

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Correct the labels
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: ancient / model / mixture / reflected light.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which is the ancient fossil?
S2. Name two different things recorded in soil C.
S3. Where does light go to make the exhibit visible?
S4. Finish one accurate museum label: “This evidence shows...”

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Produce the exhibit guide
pupilPages.intro: Use A–E. Make each reason traceable to a card.

blocks.prompt: M1. Explain why A and B need different labels.
M2. Write an accurate soil label with two components.
M3. Draw or describe the light path for D. Include the eye.
M4. What does A not tell us about the original shell?

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Challenge a confident claim
pupilPages.intro: An editor writes: “Every stone is a fossil. We know this shell’s exact colour. The dark exhibit disappeared.”

blocks.prompt: T1. Correct the first claim. What evidence of life is needed?
T2. Can card A establish the shell’s exact colour? Explain.
T3. Explain the difference between “not visible” and “not present” using E.
T4. A fresh leaf falls into soil. Explain why this alone does not make it a fossil.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. What does a fossil preserve?
E2. Name one non-mineral part of soil.
E3. What must enter the eye to see the exhibit?
R1. Which idea did you improve or defend? What evidence helped?
R2. What useful question would you investigate next?

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: 1 ancient life: remains or traces. 2 relevant soil component. 3 receive light.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 A is the ancient fossil; B is a recent model, based on their stated histories. W2 soil is a mixture, including mineral and organic material; eyes receive light from the lamp-lit exhibit.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: Second option correct. The first ignores when B was made; the third contradicts C’s organic material.

answers.label: S1–S4
answers.answer: S1 A. S2 any two recorded components: mineral grains, decayed leaf matter, air or water. S3 into the eye. S4 e.g. this fossil preserves evidence of an ancient shell; soil contains a mixture; reflected light reaches the eye.

answers.label: M1–M4
answers.answer: M1 A has geological preservation; B was made today. M2 e.g. soil contains mineral grains and organic matter, with pore spaces. M3 lamp → fossil surface → eye; arrows into eye. M4 exact original colour is unknown from this record.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 some rocks contain fossils, but a stone need not preserve remains or traces of life. T2 no: the record explicitly says unknown. T3 E states that the same fossil remains but no light reaches the eye. T4 a fresh leaf is recent organic matter; ordinary falling into soil is not evidence of ancient preservation.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 ancient remains or traces of life. E2 e.g. organic matter, water, air or a living organism. E3 light, here reflected from the exhibit.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a scientific revision, evidence-based defence or relevant next question. A private or oral response has equal value.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 7, We do 8, hinge 3, independent 12, review 3, exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the named stage time.
BUILD uses the supplied Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful contexts for older pupils. Supported, standard and stretch are selectable routes within the pathway.

Interactive We do: predict first, test against the controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. Shared W tasks offer the equivalent paper discussion. Animation is a teaching representation, not filmed experimental evidence.
Keep constructed evidence separate from actual class observations. Do not invent measurements or require internet research.
Assessment: secure core is one accurate statement from each strand and use of one actual clue. Re-teach only the weak strand; keep the pupil’s correct evidence visible.

interactive.title: Evidence editor: keep or repair?
interactive.intro: Predict, reveal the relevant scientific model, then justify one correction. Paper cards A–E provide the same evidence.
